title: Pooling: mean, CLS, and why it matters
summary: Collapsing token vectors into one is lossy, and doing it without an attention mask makes your embeddings depend on batch composition. Raw CLS vectors score worse than averaged GloVe, and no pooling choice fixes anisotropy.
html:
The encoder hands back one vector per token. A 200 token chunk comes out as 200 vectors of 768 floats. Your index needs exactly one. Something has to collapse 200 into 1, that something is called pooling, and it is a lossy reduction that people treat as an implementation detail until it costs them recall.

The options

Given token vectors h[0..n-1], each of dimension d:

StrategyWhat it doesUsed by
CLStake h[0], the vector at a special prepended tokenBERT-style classifiers, some retrievers
Meanaverage every real token vectormost sentence-transformers models
Last tokentake h[n-1]decoder-style embedders (causal attention: only the last position has seen everything)
Maxelementwise maximum across positionsrare, occasionally in older work

Mean and CLS cover almost everything you will meet, so those are the two worth understanding.

CLS, and why it is not free

BERT prepends a token called [CLS] to every input. It is not a word, and it carries no meaning of its own. It exists as a slot: a position whose vector can absorb the whole sequence through attention and then be read off as a summary.

The important part is that this only works if the training objective made it work. In original BERT, [CLS] was trained on next sentence prediction, which is a coarse, mostly binary task. It was never trained to place semantically similar sentences near one another.

The Sentence-BERT paper measured exactly this in 2019, and the result is worth remembering because it is so lopsided. On standard sentence similarity benchmarks, off-the-shelf BERT scored roughly:

CLS token                ~29
mean of token vectors    ~55
average of GloVe vectors ~58    (a 2014 method with no transformer at all)

Treat the exact figures as approximate, but the ordering is the robust and widely reproduced finding. A raw transformer's [CLS] vector is worse than averaging word vectors from a model that predates it by five years. Both are beaten by GloVe. That result is why sentence-transformers exists as a separate thing from BERT.

So CLS is not inherently bad. It is bad when nothing trained it to be good. A modern retrieval model that was explicitly trained with CLS pooling will have a perfectly good CLS vector, because the training objective (tomorrow's lesson) made it one.

Mean pooling, and the bug everyone ships once

Mean pooling averages the token vectors. It works better than it has any right to, and the reason is Day 9: these are contextualised vectors. Averaging contextualised token vectors is not the same operation as averaging static word vectors, because each one has already absorbed its neighbours. You are averaging 200 views of the sentence, not 200 isolated words.

Now the bug. Models process batches, batches need uniform length, so short sequences get padded. If you average across all positions instead of only the real ones, you are averaging in whatever the model produced at the pad positions, and that is not zero.

Here is what that does. Same four token sentence, two different batches, pooled without a mask:

batch padded to  8:  (4*real + 4*pad)  / 8
batch padded to 16:  (4*real + 12*pad) / 16

cosine of the sentence with ITSELF across those two batches:  0.894
correct masked pooling would give:                            1.000

That is a worst case, with the pad direction orthogonal to the content. Take a milder, more realistic case where the pad direction sits 30 degrees off the content and the same self-similarity comes out at 0.991.

The mild version is the dangerous one. 0.894 looks broken and you go find it. 0.991 looks fine. Nothing errors, nothing is obviously wrong, and your embeddings are quietly a function of which other documents happened to be in the batch. Re-embed the same corpus with a different batch size and you get different vectors. Recall drops a couple of points and you have no idea why.

The fix is to weight by the attention mask:

summed = (token_vectors * mask.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=1)
pooled = summed / mask.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-9)

Every serious library does this correctly. You hit it when you write the pooling yourself, which happens the moment you call a base transformer directly instead of a sentence-transformers wrapper.

The thing pooling cannot fix

Embed a hundred unrelated sentences with a raw, untuned transformer and compute all the pairwise cosines. They will cluster somewhere around 0.7 to 0.9. Everything is similar to everything.

This is anisotropy: raw contextual embeddings do not spread over the sphere, they occupy a narrow cone. If every pair scores 0.8, the ordering that scoring produces is nearly noise, which is the only thing you actually need from it.

No pooling strategy fixes this. It is a property of how the representation was trained, and the fix is to train the model so that similar things are pulled together and dissimilar things are pushed apart. That is contrastive learning, and it is tomorrow.

What to actually do

Use whatever pooling the model was trained with. That is the entire practical rule, and it is the same shape as the normalisation trap from Day 5: no error, no warning, just quietly degraded results if you mismatch.

The model card says which. If you are loading through sentence-transformers it is already configured and you should not override it. If you are calling a base transformer yourself, you are now responsible for both the pooling choice and the mask, and those are two separate opportunities to be wrong.

Ignore anyone who tells you mean is universally better than CLS. That claim traces back to the untuned-BERT result above and does not generalise to models trained for retrieval.

You have a single vector per chunk now. What remains unexplained is how the model learned to place them usefully in the first place, which is where the anisotropy goes away and the numbers start to mean something. Tomorrow: contrastive training and InfoNCE.
exercise:
1. See the anisotropy yourself. Take 20 sentences on deliberately unrelated topics. Embed them with a trained retrieval model such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2, compute all 190 pairwise cosines, and print the minimum, mean and maximum. Then do the same with a raw bert-base-uncased and your own mean pooling. Compare the two ranges. The trained model should spread; the raw one will bunch up high.

2. Reproduce the padding bug. Using a raw transformer, embed one short sentence twice: once alone, once batched with a much longer sentence. Pool without the attention mask both times and compute the cosine between the two results. It will not be 1.000. Then add the mask and confirm it is.

3. Check what your model uses. Open the model card or modules.json for whatever embedding model you plan to use and find its pooling mode. Write it down next to the normalisation setting you noted on Day 5. Those two lines are the configuration that silently decides your retrieval quality.
